extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants (U.S. patent prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claim subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101, including the two-step framework (statutory category; judicial exception analysis) and the 'markedly different characteristics' test for nature-based products with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze claims under their broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All examples are analyzed based on the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim language; examine embodiments encompassed by the claim when determining whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Determine statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is not within a statutory category, it is ineligible at Step 1; if it is, proceed to evaluate whether it is directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, or abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to an exception, proceed to Step 2B; if not directed to an exception, the claim may qualify as eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based product claims (e.g., nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, bacteria), analyze whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart(s) in their natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider structural and functional characteristics, whether differences arose from human manipulation, and whether claimed differences prevent improperly tying up natural products. If markedly different, the claim is not directed to a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess structural characteristics vs. natural counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed product has different structural characteristics (e.g., chemical bonds severed, altered nucleotide sequence, fused domains, engineered amino acid changes) compared to the natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: isolated nucleic acid with identical sequence but severed bonds was considered different structurally but not markedly different; sequence substitutions, labels attached to create a single molecule, heterologous combinations, or engineered Fc domains can provide structural differences that rise to marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess functional characteristics vs. natural counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed product exhibits different functional characteristics (e.g., encodes different protein, becomes fluorescent, altered cytotoxicity or serum half-life, changed phenotype, altered growth rate) compared to the natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional differences created by human manipulation (e.g., expression of a new marker, increased oxygen utilization, fluorescence) can contribute to a marked difference and support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation or removal alone typically insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolation or merely removing a product from its natural environment (e.g., isolating a gene or cell) does not by itself provide a marked difference if sequence/structure/function are unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Myriad, an isolated but otherwise unchanged nucleic acid is not eligible because it is not different enough from what exists in nature to avoid improperly tying up natural subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence modifications can confer marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims limited to nucleic acids having non-naturally occurring substitutions (sequence changes) can have structural differences sufficient to be markedly different from natural sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nucleic acid with changed nucleotide sequence may encode a different protein and thus be not a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment of labels or covalent modifications can confer marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a label (e.g., fluorescent label) to a nucleic acid to form a single molecule with properties not found in nature can be a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling that results in new structural and functional characteristics (e.g., fluorescence) supports ineligibility avoidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-natural combinations (e.g., vectors with heterologous sequences) confer marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining a gene with sequence(s) from another organism (vectors comprising heterologous nucleic acids) creates non-natural combinations with different genetic structure and sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such non-natural combinations can produce structural and possibly functional differences sufficient to be not a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth: if claim encompasses natural and non-natural embodiments, may be ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single claim encompasses embodiments that are structurally/functionally identical to naturally occurring items as well as changed items, the claim as a whole may lack marked difference and be a product-of-nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a broad claim to 'an antibody to Protein S' that embraces naturally occurring antibodies and engineered variants fails Step 2A because some embodiments are identical to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting claims to non-naturally occurring species (e.g., human antibodies to Protein S) can confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims specifically limited to forms not found in nature (e.g., human antibodies to an antigen where no human antibodies naturally occur) can have markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed subject matter does not exist in nature, the structural differences support that the claim is not directed to a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to specific sequences or CDRs supports eligibility unless shown to exist in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting specific complementarity determining region (CDR) sequences or SEQ ID NOs are limited to concrete molecules and are eligible unless the examiner can show that the identical molecule exists in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere possibility that nature might randomly create a similar molecule does not bar eligibility (Myriad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineered domain/variant changes (e.g., variant Fc) can provide marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to antibodies with engineered variant Fc domains comprising amino acid modifications relative to wild-type Fc domain are structurally and functionally different from natural antibodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modifications (changed cytotoxicity, serum half-life) can rise to the level of marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenotype changes from human manipulation can be markedly different (cells)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cells that are genetically identical but phenotypically different due to human manipulation (e.g., expression of marker Z, increased oxygen utilization) can be markedly different from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenotypic differences that result from applicant's efforts and confer practical advantages (e.g., improved regenerative capacity) support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population/mixture claims: emergent properties from combinations can be markedly different
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to populations or mixtures (e.g., cell populations with specific percentages or bacterial mixtures) should be analyzed for whether interactions among components give rise to properties not present in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed ratio or mixture results in emergent biological properties (e.g., altered growth rates, synergistic fermentation, lower fat yogurt), those functional differences can be a marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple unchanged components not combined do not create a marked difference (kits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting multiple naturally occurring components that are not combined (e.g., separate bacteria packets in a kit) do not change their characteristics and thus may be product-of-nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere inclusion of separate, unchanged natural species in a kit does not create marked difference because they remain unchanged and not combined in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Determine whether claim elements add 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more to the exception to transform it into eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether claimed additional features are meaningful limitations beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity, or whether they confine the claim to a particular inventive application or improve the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic, routine, and conventional limitations do not add 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of well-understood, routine, conventional items or high-level generic features (e.g., 'a container') typically does not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a container is claimed at a high level of generality and is routinely used in the art, it does not make a nature-based product claim eligible under Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination that confines claim to a particular useful application or improves technology can add 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: An element or combination that confines the claim to a particular useful application (e.g., pacemaker cells in a biocompatible scaffold that facilitates faster tissue regeneration) and improves the technology can supply significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: combining pacemaker cells with a particular scaffold to achieve a demonstrable technological improvement satisfied Step 2B (YES) and produced eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do a streamlined analysis when claim clearly does not seek to tie up natural/mineral or abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is clearly focused on an assembly, manufacturing configuration, or application that does not seek to tie up a natural product or abstract concept, a full markedly-different or abstract-idea analysis may not be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hip prosthesis assembly including hydroxyapatite (natural mineral) focuses on the assembly and does not require a full marked-difference analysis; a robotic arm claim using velocity relationships but not tying up the mathematical relationship may qualify without full analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of rare natural occurrence does not automatically defeat eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere possibility that nature might randomly create a molecule similar to one created synthetically does not render a composition nonpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Myriad, an unusual or rare natural occurrence similar to a claimed synthetic molecule does not bar eligibility if the claimed molecule is otherwise markedly different or limited to non-natural embodiments.
